metadata.title: Can Multiple AI Agents Work Better Than One?
metadata.note: STEM/AI topic-of-interest video on Agent Orchestration and Autonomous Systems. Covers: what distinguishes an 'agent' from a single LLM call (planning, tool use, iteration), what orchestration means (a controller routing work across specialized agents), the coordination pipeline, the real benefits (specialization, parallelism), and the honest risk (autonomy compounds errors across steps, so more autonomy needs more oversight, not less). Built using the same proven pattern set as prior videos: folderLabel set explicitly on ClaudeComposerAsk beats (@HumanitariansAI), OutroCTA used instead of ClaudeTitleOutro, BLUF lines kept short to avoid edge-bleed, no stale sparse_by_design flags except the legitimate BrutalistHesitantWriter typing-beat exemption.

skin_warnings: B08: palette=claude but the outro is 'OutroCTA' — OUTRO LAW wants ClaudeTitleOutro

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk — HAI persona, world-language hello (short form only)
beats.narration_text: Hi. Can a team of small AI agents actually outperform one big model doing everything itself?

props.command: claude "explain how agent orchestration coordinates multiple specialized AI agents to complete a task no single model call could handle alone"

beats.role_note: MANDATORY — BrutalistHesitantWriter, executive summary, hesitation = the pedagogy
beats.narration_text: Here's the idea. One powerful model can plan, write, and check its own work in a single pass. That sounds like all you'd ever need. It isn't — splitting the work across specialized agents, coordinated by an orchestrator, often does better.

props.text:
One strong model can plan and check its own work.
That sounds like all you'd ever need.
It isn't. Specialized agents can do better.

qc.sparse_reason: hesitant-writer typing bookend accumulates one line token by token — mid-beat frames are mostly cream by design (documented exemption case in final_frame_check.py)

beats.act: CONCEPT — what actually makes something an 'agent'
beats.role_note: vox-style illustration (C2/C3), NOT a build-loop beat
beats.narration_text: A single model call answers one prompt and stops. An agent is different: it can plan a sequence of steps, use tools, check its own output, and keep going based on what it finds — looping until the task is actually done, not just answered once.
beats.visual_intent: two cards contrasting a single model call with an agent loop

items.label: Agent
items.sub: plans, uses tools, iterates until done

beats.visual_intent: simple description card explaining the orchestrator's role
beats.narration_text: Orchestration is the layer above individual agents. An orchestrator breaks a task apart, decides which specialized agent handles which piece, passes work between them, and checks that the pieces actually add up to a finished result.

lines: An orchestrator breaks a task into pieces.
It routes each piece to the right agent.
It passes work and context between agents.
It checks the pieces add up to one result.

beats.act: THE PIPELINE — how a coordinated run actually works
beats.narration_text: As a pipeline: a task comes in. The orchestrator splits it and assigns pieces to specialized agents — say, one for research, one for drafting, one for checking the work. Each agent runs its piece. The orchestrator collects the results and assembles the final output.
beats.visual_intent: four-stage flow diagram from task through specialized agents to a combined result

props.title: One Task, Several Specialized Agents
props.footerNote: each agent handles one piece; the orchestrator assembles the whole
props.sparkLine: Divide the task. Coordinate the pieces.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: UI appears because the interface IS the subject here
beats.narration_text: Here's why this actually helps. Specialized agents can run pieces of a task in parallel instead of one after another. And if one agent's approach fails, it doesn't necessarily take the whole task down with it — the failure stays contained to that one piece.
beats.visual_intent: verdict artifact page showing the two concrete benefits

items.label: Parallelism
items.sub: independent pieces run at the same time

items.label: Fault Isolation
items.sub: one agent's failure doesn't sink the rest

beats.role_note: the lesson, honest about scope — this is where the real limitation lives
beats.narration_text: But here's the catch that matters. More autonomy means more places for something to go wrong, and errors between agents can compound instead of cancel out. A system that takes more independent action needs more oversight built in, not less — checkpoints where a human can actually see what's happening.

lines: More autonomy means more places to go wrong.
Errors between agents can compound, not cancel.
More independent action needs more oversight.
Not less human visibility — more checkpoints.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — ClaudeComposerAsk, greeting fixed to 'Your turn.', prompt read and discussed aloud
beats.narration_text: Your turn. If a task in your own work has several distinct pieces — research, drafting, checking — don't force one model call to do all of it at once. Ask Claude to help you break it into steps, with a clear checkpoint where you review before anything moves forward.
